# ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?

Haojin Wang Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign   
Yangzhen Wu Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley    Zeyi Chen
Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley    Jian Xie
Affiliation: The Ohio State University    Jiaying Ye
Affiliation: University of Washington    Lili Meng Affiliation: Google
   Shuyun Tang Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley   
Shangding Gu Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley    Dawn
Song Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley

###### Abstract

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires an agentic system to design,
train, and evaluate its own successor. Data-driven post-training is a
central part of that loop, yet existing evaluations measure it on a
single benchmark, where an agent selects from a static pool or distills
a stronger model to push one score up in one run. Real post-training is
multi-domain, and a gain in one domain has to be weighed against a
regression in another. We propose ParetoRSI-Gym, in which an agent
searches for data, curates it, trains, reads back per-domain results,
and repeats, with everything but the data held fixed: the initial LLM,
the five domains (math, code, finance, medicine, science), the toolset,
and the SFT pipeline. Generalization benchmarks in each domain separate
capability gains from overfitting to the scores the agent optimizes
against. Across three agent systems, three base models, five rounds and
multiple seeds, the strongest system, Claude Code with Opus-5, raises
the generalization scores of its proxy-best checkpoint by $`9.2\%`$
relative to the starting model ($`+2.3`$ absolute points), averaged with
equal weight over three base models and five domains, with a
single-domain relative gain of up to $`63\%`$ (medicine on
Ministral-3-3B). Further analysis shows that the harness matters as much
as the model it drives, and that each agent keeps a unique data
selection strategy. We see our work as a step towards evaluation of RSI
systems in real-world machine learning engineering.¹¹ 1 Code:
[https://github.com/haojinw0027/ParetoRSI-GYM](https://github.com/haojinw0027/ParetoRSI-GYM).

![Refer to caption](2610.34386v1/Framework.png)

Figure 1: Overview of ParetoRSI-Gym. Starting from a fixed initial
model, an agent curates post-training data for five domains over
repeated rounds. In each round the current principles direct which
datasets the agent searches for and pulls from HuggingFace, and which
entries it keeps; the resulting entries are committed to a persistent
pool, which is submitted for fine-tuning and tested on the per-domain
benchmarks; the scores are then used to update the principles for the
next round. Success requires the capability vector to expand on every
domain at once rather than on a single target.

## 1 Introduction

Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) has become a popular research direction
in modern agentic systems, where systems are designed to improve
themselves by iteratively refining their internal state ([Novikov
et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib73)). A central
pathway toward recursive self-improvement is the automation of AI
research and development: systems that can propose, implement, and
evaluate improvements to subsequent AI systems ([Schmidhuber,
2007](#bib.bib49); [Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib8); [Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib74)). Data-centric post-training is one important
component of this loop. With the advancement of AI agents, recent works
have started to explore the automation of the curation process of
post-training data ([Rank et al., 2026](#bib.bib47); [Kang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib28); [Meng et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)). For instance,
PostTrainBench ([Rank et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)) explores how well LLM
agents can perform post-training autonomously under bounded compute
constraints. Curation-Bench ([Kang et al., 2026](#bib.bib28)) evaluates
the ability of LLM agents to curate a clean dataset from a given pool of
data. RSIBench-Data ([Meng et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)) investigates
whether LLM agents can iteratively improve a dataset by adding new data
and removing incorrect entries given a target benchmark.
BenchEvolver ([Wu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib64)) instead synthesizes data:
it evolves existing coding problems into harder, verifiable tasks that
serve both as evaluation and as training signal for self-improvement. In
practice, post-training targets a set of capabilities at once: released
models are trained on mixtures spanning mathematics, code, science, and
professional domains, and are reported per capability rather than on a
single score ([Lambert et al., 2024](#bib.bib29); [Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib67); [Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib57)). Thus, instead of
evaluating the capability of modern agents in post-training data
curation for a single benchmark score, in this work, we ask: can LLM
agents curate post-training data that improves a model across multiple
capabilities at once, and keep improving it over repeated rounds of
curation?

more realistic setting for automation of post-training data curation
compared to existing benchmarks. A ✓ denotes a property enforced by the

To evaluate the current capability of LLM agents in post-training data
curation in a more realistic setting, we propose ParetoRSI-Gym, a new
benchmark for post-training data curation that evaluates the ability of
LLM agents to automatically curate post-training data for different sets
of capabilities, and continuously evolve during the post-training
process. ParetoRSI-Gym begins with a loop-like design, where agents are
required to curate data for different domains at once, and then design
training recipes based on the curated data. We define five downstream
domains for agents to curate data for: mathematics, code, science,
medical and finance. Then the agents are required to evaluate the
finetuned model on the proxy benchmarks for each domain, and then take
such feedback to iteratively refine the data curation process and the
training recipes. The agents are allowed to search, retrieve and select
data from Hugging Face, and we fix the training recipes as LoRA SFT ([Hu
et al., 2021](#bib.bib23)) and let the agents design specific training
hyperparameters for each round. To mitigate data contamination and
overfitting to the proxy benchmarks which we use as the feedback during
the curation process, we explicitly develop rejection criteria to reject
data that is close to the evaluation data, and design a held-out
generalization benchmark to evaluate the performance of the agents on
same domains but different benchmarks. This differentiates ParetoRSI-Gym
from existing benchmarks such as PostTrainBench ([Rank et al.,
2026](#bib.bib47)) and RSI-Bench Data ([Meng et al., 2026](#bib.bib39))
which evaluate the ability of agents to perform post-training on the
same benchmark. We provide a detailed comparison with existing
benchmarks in
[Tab. 1](#S1.T1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?").

We evaluate three agent systems, each combining a different harness, on
three target models drawn from different pretraining families (3B–7B),
for nine independent curation runs as main experiments. For each run we
report two checkpoints: the model from the final round, and the model
from the round whose proxy score is highest. To further understand the
behavior of the agents during the curation process, we also report the
model from the round whose proxy score is highest. Claude Code with
Opus-5 does best: at its proxy-best checkpoint, its generalization
scores are $`9.2\%`$ higher than the starting model’s in relative terms
($`+2.3`$ absolute points), averaged with equal weight over the three
base models and five domains. Gains concentrate in medical and finance,
where the largest increase at the proxy-best round is $`14.8`$ absolute
points. We also observe that the agent systems tend to peak before they
stop: in seven of the nine configurations the proxy-best round is not
the last one, indicating current agents lack the capability to robustly
continue improving the model. We further carry out a series of analysis
to understand the behavior of the agents during the curation process.
With the backbone held fixed and only the harness varied, the outcome
still ranges from $`+4.3`$ points to $`+0.2`$, highlighting the
importance of the harness in the autonomous curation process. We also
conduct a series of analysis on the dataset different agents select. We
find that two runs of the same agent overlap at $`0.24`$ Jaccard on the
datasets they select, against $`0.07`$ for different agents, indicating
that each agent keeps unique selection strategies.

Overall, our contributions are:

- •
  Multi-domain RSI benchmark. We introduce ParetoRSI-Gym, a benchmark
  for iterative, feedback-driven post-training data curation across five
  domains under bounded resource budgets.
- •
  Generalization-aware evaluation. We separate proxy feedback from
  held-out evaluation and screen training data for evaluation overlap to
  assess generalization, cross-domain trade-offs, and regressions across
  rounds.
- •
  Systematic empirical analysis. Experiments across three agent systems
  and three base models reveal transferable gains, sensitivity to
  harness design, later-round regressions, and persistent agent-specific
  data preferences.

## 2 ParetoRSI-Gym

### 2.1 Design Principles

ParetoRSI-Gym is built around five properties that reflect the
real-world post-training engineering scenario
([Tab. 1](#S1.T1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?")),
and we describe each of them in the following. Cross-round state. The
model pool, the data pool, and the written principles persist across
rounds, so what the agent commits in round $`t`$ constrains round
$`t{+}1`$. Dynamic data sources. Entries are searched for and pulled
from the HuggingFace Hub at run time rather than drawn from a
pre-assembled pool. Feedback-driven revision. Per-domain proxy results,
down to individual generations, are returned every round, and the agent
must revise its principles on that basis. Multi-domain objective. The
agent curates for $`N`$ domains at once, sees the full per-domain score
vector every round, and is asked to advance the Pareto frontier of that
vector rather than any single coordinate. Generalization evaluation.
Final scores come from generalization benchmarks the agent never
observes, which separates genuine capability gains from overfitting to
the feedback it optimizes against to mitigate the risk of reward
hacking ([Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib59)).

### 2.2 Setup

[Fig. 1](#S0.F1 "In ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?")
gives an overview of ParetoRSI-Gym. Consider a loop-like curation
process for $`N`$ domains started from an initial model $`M_{0}`$. We
first define a model pool $`\mathcal{M}=\{M_{0}\}`$ where the agent can
store the models it has curated. The agent starts from
$`\mathcal{M}=\{M_{0}\}`$, submits to a training pipeline, and is scored
by a fixed evaluation protocol. Evaluation has two parts. A proxy
benchmark set
$`\mathcal{T}_{\text{p}}=\{\mathcal{T}^{1}_{\text{p}},\dots,\mathcal{T}^{N}_{\text{p}}\}`$
reports one score per curated domain and is returned to the agent every
round. A generalization benchmark set
$`\mathcal{T}_{\text{g}}=\{\mathcal{T}^{1}_{\text{g}},\dots,\mathcal{T}^{N}_{\text{g}}\}`$
covers the capability the agent has been trained on but is never exposed
during the run. The objective of the agent is to advance the attainable
frontier of $`\mathcal{T}_{\text{p}}(M_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{N}`$ relative
to $`\mathcal{T}_{\text{p}}(M_{0})`$ rather than to raise any single
coordinate. Every round the agent receives the full vector
$`\mathbf{s}_{t}`$ for each model in $`\mathcal{M}`$ together with the
set of non-dominated checkpoints, so it never steers on a single
aggregate score. It carries three objects across rounds: the model pool
$`\mathcal{M}`$, the training pool $`P`$, whose entries record their
source and a stated reason for their commit, and a set of written
principles $`R`$ under a fixed budget $`\beta`$ for each round. Because
$`R`$ is the only channel through which evidence from one round reaches
the next, its budget bounds how much the agent can accumulate.

### 2.3 Data Curation Loop

We develop a loop-like curation system that allows the agent to improve
the model capability in a realistic post-training engineering scenario.
To begin with, the agent is given $`\mathcal{M}=\{M_{0}\}`$ and its
initial capability vector
$`\mathbf{s}_{0}=\mathcal{T}_{\text{p}}(M_{0})`$. The agent then writes
an initial set of principles as $`R_{0}`$ based on the initial
capability vector $`\mathbf{s}_{0}`$ and the budget $`\beta_{0}`$. After
that, it starts to curate the post-training data pool $`P`$ for each
domain based on the data principle $`R_{0}`$ and the budget
$`\beta_{0}`$. All data come from the HuggingFace Hub, and the agent
reaches it through three operations. Search queries the Hub by keywords,
tags, and dataset metadata, and returns candidate datasets with their
cards. Select picks which of these datasets, and which splits or subsets
of them, are worth acquiring. Pull downloads the selected data so the
agent can inspect the entries and add those it keeps to the pool. The
agent decides what to search for and what to pull based on the data
principle $`R_{0}`$, within the budget $`\beta_{0}`$.

After the first round data pool $`P`$ is curated, the agent fine-tunes
the base model $`M_{0}`$ on $`P`$ through the training pipeline
$`\mathcal{S}`$ along with a training config $`\mathcal{C}`$ to get the
first round model $`M_{1}`$, and adds $`M_{1}`$ to the model pool
$`\mathcal{M}`$. The agent then evaluates the first round model
$`M_{1}`$ on the per-domain benchmarks $`\mathcal{T}_{\text{p}}`$ to get
the first round capability vector
$`\mathbf{s}_{1}=\mathcal{T}_{\text{p}}(M_{1})`$. After the first round,
the agent first decides which model to use for the next round based on
current model pool $`\mathcal{M}`$. The agent then updates the
principles for the next round according to the proxy evaluation,
updating data pool $`P`$ and training the chosen model $`M_{t-1}`$ from
$`\mathcal{M}`$ on $`P`$. The loop continues for $`T`$ rounds. We
finally report the performance of two checkpoints on the generalization
benchmarks. We first report the final round model as the final
evaluation result. We also report the model with best proxy score as the
proxy-best evaluation result. A detailed description of the loop is
provided in
[App. A](#A1 "Appendix A The Curation Loop ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?").

### 2.4 Evaluation

The evaluation of ParetoRSI-Gym is conducted in two parts. The first
part is the proxy evaluation, which is used during training to guide the
agent to curate data. The second part is the generalization evaluation
which is distinct from the proxy evaluation to avoid overfitting or data
contamination.
[Tab. 2](#S3.T2 "In 3.1 Model ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?")
lists both suites: each pair targets the same capability but shares no
item, and for code the held-out suite is a separate benchmark. We report
accuracy on the generalization benchmarks.

Because the reported score comes from $`\mathcal{T}_{\text{g}}`$, full
access to $`\mathcal{T}_{\text{p}}`$ does not expose the items we report
on, so we return the whole evaluation trace rather than one number per
domain. The agent receives not only the proxy scores but also the
evaluation trace of the model on the proxy benchmarks. It can therefore
attribute a failure to a missing skill or to a format mismatch, and
rewrite its principles against that evidence instead of steering on five
scalars. The generalization suite is never exposed during the run and is
scored only after the final round, under the same decoding protocol. A
model that gains on the proxy without gaining there has fitted the
feedback rather than the capability, and we report the two scores
separately.

## 3 Experiments

### 3.1 Model

To start the experiments, we use three different base models and one
instruction-tuned model, ranging from different families of models:
Qwen3-4B-Base ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib67)),
Ministral-3-3B-Base-2512 ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib34)), and
Olmo-3-1025-7B ([Olmo et al., 2025](#bib.bib43)). Such design choice
reflects the real-world practice of post-training, where the base model
is first pre-trained on large scale data, and then finetuned on
domain-specific data by downstream users. We intentionally choose
different base models from different families to mitigate the effect of
model family bias. We also include models with various sizes to measure
whether the agent systems can identify different patterns of improvement
across different model sizes.

| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- |

| Science | GPQA ID ([Rein et al., 2023](#bib.bib48))                    | GPQA OOD ([Rein et al., 2023](#bib.bib48))                    |
| Medical | MedBullets ID ([Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib5))               | MedBullets OOD ([Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib5))               |
| Finance | SuperGPQA Finance ID ([M-A-P Team et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)) | SuperGPQA Finance OOD ([M-A-P Team et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)) |
| Code    | MBPP+ ([Austin et al., 2021](#bib.bib3))                     | HumanEval + ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib7))                  |

Table 3: Main results of ParetoRSI-Gym on the generalization benchmarks.
Each cell is the score followed by its change in points from the

### 3.2 Research Agents

We evaluate three research agents that pair a harness with a backbone
model: Claude Code ([Anthropic, 2025](#bib.bib1)) with
Opus-5 ([Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib2)), Codex ([OpenAI,
2025](#bib.bib44)) with GPT-5.6 Sol ([OpenAI, 2026](#bib.bib45))
(reasoning effort: medium), and CheetahClaw ([Team, 2026](#bib.bib53))
with deepseek-v4-flash ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib66)). Each agent runs
fully autonomously with all tool calls auto-approved, inside a sandbox
whose network access is restricted to the HuggingFace Hub; the
generalization benchmarks are never present in its environment. All
rounds of a run are carried out in a single agent session: at the start
of each round the session is resumed with the new proxy results, so the
agent retains its full interaction history from earlier rounds alongside
the model pool, the data pool, and the written principles.

### 3.3 Training Details

Each round fine-tunes the checkpoint the agent selects with LoRA ([Hu
et al., 2021](#bib.bib23)) and AdamW ([Loshchilov and Hutter,
2017](#bib.bib35)), for one epoch over the submitted pool. The agent
chooses the learning rate, LoRA rank, batch size, sequence length and
warmup within a fixed range; the rest of the pipeline is frozen. Each
round is capped at $`15`$M training tokens and $`40`$k entries, and a
run lasts five rounds. Following PostTrainBench ([Rank et al.,
2026](#bib.bib47)), we repeat every Claude Code and Codex configuration
with three training seeds and report the mean across seeds; for open
source systems such as CheetahClaw we run once per base model.

Figure 2: Proxy gains generalize to held-out benchmarks. We present the
trend of the proxy gains and the generalization gains of model during
training process on Qwen3-4B-Base with Codex and GPT-5.6 Sol. Proxy
gains during training directly translate to generalization gains on the
held-out benchmarks, indicating that the agent system is capable of
curating post-training data for healthy post-training performance.

### 3.4 Main Results

We present the main results of the experiments in
[Tab. 3](#S3.T3 "In 3.1 Model ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?").
For each agent run for each base model, we report three values for each
domain. _Final_ means the final model performance on the generalization
benchmarks after the last round of training. _Proxy Best_ is the
checkpoint whose average proxy score is the highest, scored on the
generalization benchmarks. _Domain best_ means the best performance of
the models in the loop on the generalization benchmarks for the
corresponding domain.

#### Agent systems differ in how much they improve the model.

Averaged over the five domains and the three base models, the proxy-best
checkpoint gains $`+2.3`$ points over the starting model with Claude
Code, $`+0.6`$ with Codex, and $`-0.3`$ with CheetahClaw. In relative
terms, computing $`(s-s_{M_{0}})/s_{M_{0}}`$ for each base model and
domain and averaging the fifteen values with equal weight, the gains are
$`+9.2\%`$, $`+3.1\%`$ and $`+2.9\%`$; the relative figure weights
low-baseline cells heavily, so we report both. The largest relative
gain, $`+63\%`$ on medicine with Ministral-3-3B
($`23.65\rightarrow 38.46`$), starts from a base model that often does
not end its answer with an option letter, so part of this gain is the
model learning the answer format rather than medical knowledge. We find
that the performance gain over different domains is not consistent. The
agents tend to improve the performance of the models on medical (4.3
absolute points) and code (3.2 absolute points) benchmarks, while the
performance on math behaves differently as training downgrades the
performance, and we conduct a detailed case analysis in
[§​ D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Failure Case on Mathematical Reasoning ‣ Appendix D Case Studies ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?").
We also observe that the different base models have different patterns
of improvement. The agents tend to improve more on Ministral-3-3B than
on Qwen3-4B-Base and Olmo-3-1025-7B, indicating a high model-dependent
effect of the current agent systems on autonomous post-training.

#### Later curation rounds can undo the gains of earlier ones.

As the training process continues, the agent system may not maintain the
performance gain over previous rounds on different domains
simultaneously. Across 5 domains over the 9 different agent-model
setups, 24 out of 45 settings experience a performance drop comparing to
the performance of the round with the highest proxy gain. After gaining
performance on the proxy benchmarks, what the agent system plans to do
next is not guaranteed to be translated into further performance gain.
It may even undo the gains of previous rounds, suggesting that modern
agentic systems have a price to pay for exploration: the checkpoint they
hand back is often not the best one they have produced.
[Section D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 A Round That Improves Every Domain ‣ Appendix D Case Studies ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?")
follows one run in which a single round improves every domain at once
and later rounds give part of that back.

#### No single round is best for all domains.

The per-domain best row is an oracle: for each domain we take the
highest accuracy on the generalization benchmarks any round reached,
which allows a different checkpoint per domain and is therefore not a
deliverable model. Comparing it with the proxy-best row separates two
costs, curating badly and having to hand back one model for five
domains. The second is almost universal: in $`43`$ of the $`45`$
model–domain cells the best round for a domain is not the round the
agent selects, at a cost of $`2.0`$ points on average and up to $`6.9`$.
This suggests that the current agent systems do not have enough
capability to promote the pareto frontier of the model capabilities
which sustains already obtained capabilities while exploring new
capabilities.

## 4 Analysis

The main results in
[Tab. 3](#S3.T3 "In 3.1 Model ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?")
report the endpoints of a run: the checkpoints an agent hands back after
five rounds. They leave open what happens inside a run, and which part
of an agent system is responsible for the difference between systems. We
therefore ask three questions. First, we follow a run round by round and
ask whether the proxy scores the agent steers by move together with the
generalization scores we report. Second, we hold the backbone fixed and
vary only the harness, which separates what the scaffold contributes
from what the model driving it contributes. Third, we look inside the
training pools: which datasets each agent selects, how far different
agents overlap, and when they stop searching for new sources.

### 4.1 Trend Analysis

Figure 4: The checkpoint each round is trained from. Share of the rounds
after the first that restart from $`M_{0}`$, branch from an earlier
round, or continue from the round before.

We present a study of trend analysis in
[Fig. 2](#S3.F2 "In 3.3 Training Details ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?").
We analyze with Qwen3-4B-Base as the base model for ParetoRSI-Gym
training and Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol as the agent system. We find that
the proxy gains during training move in the same direction as the
generalization gains on the generalization benchmarks. Across different
domains, the two signals do not move by the same amount. On code the
proxy gains stay within 3 points of the starting model, while the
generalzation gains reach 11 points. We also observe how the agent
system handles the proxy benchmark feedback by selecting different
checkpoints for each round in
[Fig. 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.1 Trend Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?").
Claude Code and Codex tend to continue curating from an earlier
checkpoint, in $`64\%`$ and $`53\%`$ of their rounds, while CheetahClaw
starts from scratch in $`67\%`$ of its own rounds and never branches
back to an older round at all.

### 4.2 Harness Performance

Figure 5: Harnesses with a fixed backbone. Change in generalization
accuracy relative to $`M_{0}`$ at each harness’s proxy-best checkpoint
(in parentheses); DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Max on Qwen3-4B-Base, one run
each.

We analyze the performance of the same agent backbone with different
harnesses to study the contribution of the harness to the autonomous
post-training performance ([Gu, 2026](#bib.bib18)). To study this, we
fix the backbone model as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Max ([Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib66)) and vary the harness to be claude code, codex and
cheetah claw. We present the performance of the model at the proxy-best
checkpoint for each harness in
[Fig. 5](#S4.F5 "In 4.2 Harness Performance ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?").
We observe that different harnesses produce different results. On
average, Codex produces the best results of 4.3 gains on the
generalization benchmarks, followed by Claude Code with 2.6 points and
CheetahClaw with 0.2 points. On average, the agent systems contribute
most significantly to the performance gain on coding domains, with the
highest gains by Codex with 13.2 points. This indicates that autonomous
post-training performance should not only consider developing stronger
models but also consider carefully crafting the harnesses to match model
capabilities, so that better design of the harness can complement the
strength of the model.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 4.3 Agent Decision-Making

We further investigate the details of the agent decision-making process
on dataset selection for post-training. In
[Fig. 3](#S4.F3 "In 4 Analysis ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?"),
we present the datasets each agent selects into its training pool across
runs and rounds. We first observe that each agent has a preferred
dataset taste. Two runs of the same agent reach a Jaccard overlap of
0.24 on their dataset lists, against 0.07 for two runs of different
agents, and the overlap does not rise when the two runs also share a
base model (0.23 within a base model against 0.25 across base models).
This suggests that what an agent reaches for is set by the agent itself
and carries over unchanged to a new target model, suggesting that
current agent systems do not adapt to the target model. Second, we
observe that the share of training data of different domains is
consistent. Averaged over runs, the domain shares barely move from round
to round. Individual runs are much less even: one Codex run devotes its
entire final pool to code, and one CheetahClaw run gives medical over
$`80\%`$ of two of its rounds. Finally, fewer and fewer datasets enter
the pool for the first time as the run goes on. This suggests that
current agent systems behave statically as the task horizon progresses:
the agent is no longer willing to explore new sources of data to promote
performance gains in later rounds.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 5 Related Work

### 5.1 Data Curation Benchmarks.

Early data curation benchmarks score a curation pipeline by the
downstream performance of the model it produces ([Mazumder et al.,
2023](#bib.bib38); [Gadre et al., 2023](#bib.bib16); [Li et al.,
2024](#bib.bib31)). Recent work hands the pipeline to an agent:
CurationBench ([Kang et al., 2026](#bib.bib28)) has it select from a
fixed pool, PostTrainBench ([Rank et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)) gives it a
base model and a benchmark and lets it post-train against that
benchmark, RSIBench-Data ([Meng et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)) closes the
loop on one benchmark, CurateEvo ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib58))
evolves the curation policy itself, BenchEvolver ([Wu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib64)) evolves reference solutions into harder verifiable
coding tasks for evaluation and training, and [Chi et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib10) move the object of improvement from the data to the
training algorithm. ParetoRSI-Gym requires agents to focus on multiple
domains simultaneously during the agentic data loop, allowing agents to
select from dynamic data, and using generalization benchmarks to
evaluate the genuine capability promotion.

### 5.2 Recursive Self-Improvement Systems.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to the Gödel
machine ([Schmidhuber, 2007](#bib.bib49)), which rewrites its own code
only under a proof of benefit. LLM-based agents relax that proof into
empirical validation, editing their own scaffold and keeping whichever
variant scores higher ([Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib36); [Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib73)); later work makes the editing mechanism itself
editable ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib74)), shares experience across a
population ([Weng et al., 2026](#bib.bib62)), co-evolves the agent with
its evaluator ([Iacob et al., 2026](#bib.bib24)), turns the loop on
algorithm discovery ([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)), or lets
several models improve one another by distilling their collaboration
back into each model ([Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)). Work on
harnesses reports that a loop tuned on its own evolution split transfers
only partly to tasks it never saw ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib65); [Wu
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib63); [Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib59)), while a
second route leaves the scaffold alone and updates the model’s weights
instead ([Hebbar et al., 2026](#bib.bib21)). ParetoRSI-Gym instead fits
into the RSI framework by benchmarking the capability of agent systems
in diverse domain post-training data curation, which is critical for RSI
systems to achieve better automation in real-world data curation.

## 6 Conclusion

We present ParetoRSI-Gym, a benchmark for evaluating the capability of
modern LLM-based AI agents in post-training curation of realistic tasks.
Instead of focusing on data curation to lift performance on a single
benchmark, ParetoRSI-Gym aims to evaluate by focusing on curation of
multiple domains reflecting the real-world post-training scenario. To
further mitigate the caveat of data contamination, ParetoRSI-Gym
introduces proxy benchmarks and generalization benchmarks to avoid
overfitting to the domains it seen during curation. Across multiple
experiments on ParetoRSI-Gym with different agent systems and base
models, we observe that current agent systems can form a curation
strategy from the feedback they see, yet lacking the capability of
continuously improving the model, and often hand back suboptimal
checkpoints. Through further analysis, we find that the different agent
systems have their own preferences in data selection, and different
harnesses matter for successful post-training automation. We hope
ParetoRSI-Gym serves as a first step towards more realistic and
comprehensive evaluation of post-training automation.

## Limitations

Our work can be extended in several ways. First, we only experiment with
three agent systems and three base models. Future work can continue to
explore different agent systems and models with larger scales, which
could study the capability of current agent systems in broader
scenarios. Second, the three agent systems are moving targets. Our
results are a snapshot of the harness and backbone versions available at
the time of writing. Third, we cover five domains and only English text.
We leave the exploration of other languages and domains for future work.
We hope this work serves as a first step towards more realistic and
comprehensive evaluation of post-training automation.

## Ethics Statement

We use only public datasets and published benchmarks, collect no user
data, and run agents sandboxed with every entry screened against the
evaluation items; nonetheless, agents choose their training data
autonomously, inheriting the biases of the sources they reach for and
adding a selection bias of their own; thus any real-world use should
include bias audits, content filtering, and strict dataretention
controls.

## Appendix A The Curation Loop

The loop each run follows is stated below;
[§​ 2](#S2 "2 ParetoRSI-Gym ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?")
describes it in prose.

1: initial model $`M_{0}`$; agent $`\mathcal{A}`$; training pipeline
$`\mathcal{S}`$; proxy suite $`\mathcal{T}_{\text{proxy}}`$ over $`N`$
domains; generalization suite $`\mathcal{T}_{\text{general}}`$;
per-round budget $`\beta`$; horizon $`T`$

2: $`\mathcal{M}\leftarrow\{M_{0}\}`$,  $`P\leftarrow\emptyset`$, 
$`\mathbf{s}_{0}\leftarrow\mathcal{T}_{\text{proxy}}(M_{0})`$, 
$`R_{0}\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{s}_{0})`$ $`\triangleright`$
$`\mathcal{M}`$, $`P`$ and $`R`$ are the only state that crosses rounds

3: for $`t=1,\dots,T`$ do

4:   $`P\leftarrow P\cup\mathcal{A}.\textsc{Acquire}(R_{t-1})`$
$`\triangleright`$ Search, Select and Pull on the Hub; entries keep
their source and $`P`$ only grows

5:
  $`M^{\text{par}},\,D_{t},\,\mathcal{C}_{t}\leftarrow\mathcal{A}.\textsc{Commit}(\mathcal{M},P,R_{t-1})`$
$`\triangleright`$ parent checkpoint, training set and recipe, within
$`\beta`$

6:
  $`M_{t}\leftarrow\mathcal{S}(M^{\text{par}},D_{t};\mathcal{C}_{t})`$, 
$`\mathcal{M}\leftarrow\mathcal{M}\cup\{M_{t}\}`$

7:   $`\mathbf{s}_{t},E_{t}\leftarrow\mathcal{T}_{\text{proxy}}(M_{t})`$
$`\triangleright`$ per-domain scores and per-item results, both returned
to the agent

8:   $`R_{t}\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(R_{t-1},\mathbf{s}_{0:t},E_{t})`$
$`\triangleright`$ principles rewritten from the evidence, under the
same $`\beta`$

9: end for

10: return $`\mathcal{T}_{\text{general}}(M_{T})`$ and
$`\mathcal{T}_{\text{general}}(M_{t^{\star}})`$, where
$`t^{\star}=\arg\max_{t}\operatorname{mean}(\mathbf{s}_{t})`$
$`\triangleright`$ scored once, after the run

Loop 1 Multi-domain data curation in ParetoRSI-Gym.

We present a typical round of how a agent curates a dataset in practice.
Below is a transcript of a round of Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol on
Olmo-3-1025-7B, round 2. This reflects the typical workflow of a agent
curating a dataset in practice.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Two steps carry most of what the later sections examine. Step 7 is where
an agent decides whether a run accumulates or restarts, and the agents
differ sharply on it. Step 6 is where the pool is fixed, and the zero in
it holds for $`49`$ of the $`50`$ rounds we logged: an agent settles the
fate of tens of thousands of entries without reading one of them.

## Appendix D Case Studies

### D.1 Failure Case on Mathematical Reasoning

We observe that in
[Tab. 3](#S3.T3 "In 3.1 Model ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?")
that most of the agents fail to improve the capability of the original
model on mathematical reasoning tasks. In this section we provide a
detailed case study of this to understand the failure mode of the
agents. We study the run of Claude Code with Opus-5 on Olmo-3-1025-7B,
where math falls by $`20.1`$ points in the first round and recovers
above $`M_{0}`$ in the second, with both rounds trained from the base
model under the same recipe. We observe that the agents tend to select
datasets with shorter answer lengths such as NuminaMath ([LI et al.,
2024](#bib.bib32)) in the earliest rounds, where the original model
tends to generate longer answers. Such behavior is detrimental to the
improvement of the model on mathematical reasoning tasks, since the
model gains accuracy by generating longer answers. In later rounds, the
agents tend to change its strategy of dataset selection to select
datasets with answers of similar length to the original model, usually
datasets with longer reasoning chains ([Moshkov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib40)). The selection record from the agent also shows the
incentive at work: in the first round it filters NuminaMath ([LI et al.,
2024](#bib.bib32)) datasets for “concise math CoT ($`\leq`$5k chars) to
finish solutions within budget”, since a token-denominated budget buys
more entries when the answers are short. In the second round it discards
that lineage and pulls long \<think\> traces instead, recovering math
with a seventh of the entries.

Figure 6: Answer length and math accuracy over the rounds.

### D.2 Forming Experience While Curating

In the execution of ParetoRSI-Gym, the agent forms experience while
curating the datasets by weaving its own observations into the notes
file. Such note files document how agent forms its own beliefs with
prior experiences and observations on the proxy benchmark. In the box
below, we present a case study of the agent’s experience formation while
curating the finance domain in the run of Claude Code with Opus-5 on
Olmo-3-1025-7B.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We observe that the agent forms its own useful experience and leads to
continuous improvement during later rounds. In this case, after first
round of curation, the agent forms a belief that the 10-option
OpenScience ([NVIDIA, 2025](#bib.bib42)) econ traces are the most
effective for the finance domain after observing that finance is the
only domain whose answers keep their long reasoning style after round 1,
at $`2{,}279`$ tokens against $`65`$–$`718`$ elsewhere. In the third
round, the agent further forms a belief that shorter traces should help,
and acts on it in the round that follows. This experience helps the
agent to further improve the finance accuracy to $`0.250`$, the best in
the run, suggesting that the agent’s experience formation is effective
in guiding its curation strategy.

### D.3 A Round That Improves Every Domain

We provide a case from our runs in which the agent pushes the Pareto
frontier forward:
[Fig. 7](#A4.F7 "In D.3 A Round That Improves Every Domain ‣ Appendix D Case Studies ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?")
follows Claude Code with Opus-5 on Ministral-3-3B. Round 2 continues
from round 1 and trades medicine for math and code: it gains on both but
loses $`7.8`$ points on medicine. The agent then discards round 2:
round 3 branches back from round 1 and rebuilds its medical data, and
the resulting checkpoint is at least as good as $`M_{0}`$ on every
generalization benchmark, significantly better on medicine and code, and
also the round with the highest proxy score. The improvement does not
persist: rounds 4 and 5 keep the medical and code gains but give back
math, so the final checkpoint no longer dominates $`M_{0}`$. The loop
can thus reach a Pareto improvement over the starting model, and holding
on to it is harder than finding it.

![Refer to caption](2610.34386v1/case_pareto.png)

Figure 7: Change on the generalization benchmarks relative to $`M_{0}`$,
in points, for Claude Code with Opus-5 on Ministral-3-3B. Each column is
one round’s checkpoint and the checkpoint it was trained from. $`*`$
marks a change whose 95% paired bootstrap interval over items excludes
zero. The boxed round is at least as good as $`M_{0}`$ in every domain.

## Appendix F Human Baseline

We compare the agents with human supervision within the curation loop of
ParetoRSI-Gym
([algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Appendix A The Curation Loop ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?")).
The agent searches for and pulls candidate datasets from the Hugging
Face Hub as in a regular run, and a human then takes over the commit
step: the human reviews the entries the agent pulled and decides which
of them enter the training pool, under the same token budget, training
pipeline and evaluation as the agents.
[Table 7](#A6.T7 "In Appendix F Human Baseline ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?")
reports the result on the three base models beside $`M_{0}`$ and the
strongest agent.

|                |                                  |       |         |         |         |       |
| -------------- | -------------------------------- | ----- | ------- | ------- | ------- | ----- |
| Base Model     | Model                            | Math  | Science | Medical | Finance | Code  |
| Qwen3-4B-Base  | $`M_{0}`$                        | 65.33 | 31.94   | 39.36   | 24.50   | 65.03 |
|                | Claude Code + Opus-5, Proxy Best | 60.97 | 33.33   | 43.69   | 24.50   | 71.93 |
|                | Human supervised                 | 72.50 | 25.88   | 40.37   | 28.00   | 65.95 |
| Ministral-3-3B | $`M_{0}`$                        | 38.92 | 27.65   | 23.65   | 17.62   | 26.69 |
|                | Claude Code + Opus-5, Proxy Best | 34.64 | 29.00   | 38.46   | 19.63   | 39.26 |
|                | Human supervised                 | 65.67 | 19.70   | 39.70   | 20.00   | 50.46 |
| Olmo-3-1025-7B | $`M_{0}`$                        | 71.08 | 22.73   | 32.43   | 18.25   | 48.01 |
|                | Codex + GPT-5.6 Sol, Proxy Best  | 69.50 | 24.92   | 30.41   | 19.00   | 49.90 |
|                | Human supervised                 | 68.00 | 24.37   | 32.94   | 24.25   | 48.93 |

Table 7: Human baseline on the generalization benchmarks. $`M_{0}`$ and
agent rows are taken from
[Tab. 3](#S3.T3 "In 3.1 Model ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?");
the agent row is the agent whose _Proxy Best_ checkpoint has the highest
mean on that base model.

Human in the loop remains crucial for current agent systems to improve a
model across domains. Human supervision reaches gains that no agent
reaches, most clearly on math for Qwen3-4B-Base and Ministral-3-3B and
on finance for Olmo-3-1025-7B, and on average it matches or exceeds the
strongest agent on every base model. This motivates future RSI systems
to keep humans in the curation loop and learn from their decisions,
rather than curating fully autonomously.
